_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: It is written with regard to affordability: about one who says, “My valuation is upon me,” and does not have enough for the valuation, it is written: “according to the means of him who vowed shall the priest value him” (Leviticus 27:8), and after it is written: “And all your valuations [shall be with the shekel of the Sanctuary]” (Leviticus 27:25), [to teach] that even if he does not have a shekel’s worth, the priest may not value him at less than a shekel.
rashi:a2.1: The halakha is in accordance with the statement of the Rabbis: that it is redeemed with a lamb of any value.
rashi:a2.3: Bar danka: a small one, worth only a ma’a, which is a sixth of a dinar.
rashi:a2.4: We learn as well: in our mishna.
rashi:a3.1: It is obvious: that even a patruza [may be used], since the Rabbis said above “any amount.”
rashi:a3.2: So far as this: [as little as] a bar danka. Alternatively: granted that one may give a small one, but not a patruza, which is lean.
rashi:a5.1: Close here and close here: less than a sela and more than a shekel.
rashi:a6.1: The halakha contradicts the halakha: here you said the halakha is a ragya, and above you said the halakha is in accordance with the statement of the Rabbis, that even a bar danka [suffices].
rashi:a6.2: To one who comes to consult: about what to give the priest, we tell him: a ragya.
rashi:a6.3: To one who acts on his own: and gives a bar danka, we do not compel him [to give] more.
rashi:a7.1: Doesn’t he say: in our discussion above (Bekhorot 9b), that the Torah was particular about him with a lamb. And even though we answered above that it does not speak of [redeeming] at its value, still, the one raising the difficulty here takes what was initially assumed.
rashi:a8.1: Ravina found it difficult: why do you establish Reish Lakish’s statement according to Rabbi Shimon? We hold that [in a dispute of] Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon the halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, [as stated] in Eruvin, in chapter Mi SheHotziuhu (Eruvin 46b). And the tanna of our mishna taught us an unattributed ruling in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, who prohibits benefit from a firstborn donkey, since it teaches that he designates a lamb to abrogate its prohibition.
rashi:a9.1: And you say: [you establish] your statement according to Rabbi Shimon.
rashi:a10.1: More stringent than consecrated items: which one redeems with money at its value.
rashi:a10.2: To be stringent with him: that he may redeem it only with a lamb.
rashi:a10.3: But to be lenient with him: that if he redeems it with a lamb, he may redeem it [even] with a patruza.
rashi:a12.1: It is the property of the owner: and the priest cannot sell it to this redeemer; his redemption is redeemed for the owner, and this one has left his money on the horn of a deer [i.e., it is lost to him].
rashi:a13.1: And he will give the money: as it is written, “And if he who consecrated it will redeem it…” (Leviticus 27:19); this implies that whoever gives the money, the consecrated item will be his.
rashi:a13.2: Or perhaps, since he acquires: the owner acquires this firstborn donkey for the in-between [amount], since he can redeem it with a lamb. Even though he does not acquire all of it as long as he has not redeemed it, even so it is his property.
rashi:a14.1: And even though he does not have it now: that is, even though he has no right [to it] now, he has [a right] later, when he redeems it; therefore it is as if it is his now.
rashi:a16.1: “And it be stolen from the man’s house,” states the Merciful One: he shall pay double; not from the house of the Temple, since there is no double payment for consecrated property.
rashi:a18.1: You cannot say where it came into the possession of a priest: if the Israelite gave it to the priest, it no longer enters [the pen] to be tithed, neither in the priest’s possession nor in the Israelite’s, even if the Israelite went back and bought it from him, or the priest gave it to him, for we learned, etc.
rashi:a18.2: Uncertain firstborn donkeys: for example, he had ten female donkeys and each of them bore a male and a female, so he designates ten lambs for them to abrogate their prohibition, and he tithes them like other non-sacred animals, and they are his. And the tithe animal is offered as a peace offering and he eats it, according to the law of other animal tithe.
rashi:a20.1: And that mother’s father, a priest, they had been bequeathed to him, etc.: for then they are obligated in redemption, since they were born in the domain of an Israelite.
rashi:a21.1: He designates ten lambs for them: to abrogate their prohibition.
rashi:a21.2: And they are his: for what the priest who bequeathed them was obligated to do with them, this one does with them. The bequeathing priest would have had to designate lambs for them, to abrogate the sanctity that took effect on them in the house of the first Israelite, and he would take the lambs for himself, since he is a priest and need not seek out a priest. So too this Israelite who inherits from him does, for it is as if the priest bequeathed the lambs to him.
rashi:a22.1: Smoothed: whose processing is complete with regard to tithe, for smoothing is the completion of the work of grain, when one levels the pile and smooths it with a winnowing shovel.
rashi:a22.2: And that mother’s father, a priest, etc.: it teaches us a novelty. Even though it comes by virtue of an Israelite, so that one could say he should now give the teruma (and tithe) to a priest, just as the first Israelite would have done, even so, since a priest’s hand is in between, it is as if the middle priest separated the teruma from it and bequeathed [the produce and the gifts] to this Israelite each by itself. So he tithes them and it is all his, and he sells the teruma to priests. And the same applies even if they had not come to that priest from an Israelite, for a priest’s grain is obligated in teruma, except that he does not give it to another priest but separates it and eats it.
rashi:a23.1: Because it stands separated: that is, the lamb is one kind and the donkey another, and no act is lacking. Therefore it is as if the donkeys came to him from the priest’s house by themselves and the lambs by themselves.
rashi:a24.1: But: with grain, which lacks separation, say that they are regarded as not separated in the priest’s house, and they revert to their original prohibition, and he should give them to a priest.
tosafot:a2.1: Rava said: We learn as well, “big or small”: some books read “we learned” [tenina, without “we too”], and then this is a question [i.e., the mishna already teaches it, so why did Rav Yosef need to say it?].
tosafot:a5.1: And the halakha is with a ragya: we establish it as referring to one who comes to consult, whom we instruct to redeem it with a lamb worth three zuz, “close here [and close there]”; but [one who acts] on his own [may use] even a lean lamb worth a danka. And if he has no lamb to redeem it, he redeems it at its value, even with boiled vegetables. And when he redeems it, he recites the blessing over the redemption of a firstborn donkey [then], and not at the time of giving it to the priest, for from the moment he separated it, it stands in the priest’s possession, as is said below in our discussion. And the lamb may be from sheep or from goats, male or female, big or small, as we learned in the mishna.
tosafot:a11.1: One who redeems the firstborn donkey of another, his redemption is redeemed: this is not like one who separates teruma from his own produce for another’s, about which a dilemma was raised in chapter Ein Bein HaMudar (Nedarim 36b) whether [the owner’s] consent is required. For there it is written “you also” (Numbers 18:28), to include your agent, and we require: just as you [separate] with your consent, so your agent with your consent. But here “owner” is not written.
tosafot:a16.1: “And it be stolen from the man’s house,” and not from the house of the Temple: in chapter Merubba (Bava Kamma 62b) this exposition appears where it says that it is derived from “his neighbor” (Exodus 22:8), and not from consecrated property. And it explains that “man” is not superfluous, since the Temple treasurer is also called a man; and nothing at all can be excluded from “man,” since the word “man” applies to anything that is masculine, and “woman” to the feminine, as in “one [isha] to another [ahota]” (Exodus 26:3). And what is said here, “from the man’s house and not from the house of the Temple,” is as derived from “his neighbor”; it cites this verse because the verse “and it be stolen” speaks of payment.
tosafot:a18.1: An Israelite who had ten uncertain [firstborn] donkeys designates ten lambs and tithes them and they are his: according to Rabbeinu Tam, who explained above that “he redeems again even many times” refers to cases of uncertainty, it is difficult: why do I need ten lambs? One lamb would suffice. But according to the explanation of the Kuntres [Rashi], that he does not redeem again unless he gave it to a priest and took it back, it works out. However, according to his explanation too, the case below is difficult: an Israelite who had ten certain firstborn donkeys in his house that were bequeathed to him from the household of his mother’s father, a priest, and that mother’s father, a priest, had them bequeathed from the household of his mother’s father, an Israelite: he designates ten lambs for them and they are his. There, why do I need ten? One suffices, since by law they are his even though they are certain [firstborns]; so each time it is regarded as if he gave it to a priest and took it back, since he inherits by virtue of his mother’s father, a priest. It seems, then, that in all these cases he says “ten” as a novelty: even though all of them are [lambs for] firstborn donkeys, they all enter the pen to be tithed.
gershom:a1.1: And how much? Any amount, even a patruza bar danka: even a lean lamb worth only a sixth of the shekel [Rashi: a sixth of a dinar].
gershom:a2.1: This is how we read: Rava said: We learned in the mishna “big or small, unblemished or blemished.” Lest you say that the mishna did not mean so far as a bar danka, or alternatively did not mean a patruza that is lean, Rav Yosef teaches us. Rabbi Tarfon was a priest.
gershom:a3.1: With a ragya. And how much is a ragya? Three zuz. And that is the explanation of the word ragya: “close here and close here,” that is, near to this and near to that, for three zuz is short of a sela by only one zuz, and more than a shekel by only one zuz.
gershom:a4.1: The halakha contradicts the halakha: for above we established even a patruza bar danka, and here he says the halakha is a ragya.
gershom:a5.1: Here, where he comes to consult: [if he asks] how much he should give, we tell him a ragya. Where he comes on his own, if he redeemed it of his own accord with a danka, it is redeemed.
gershom:a6.1: If we say according to Rabbi Yehuda: who said the Torah was particular about him with a lamb, as was initially assumed: with a lamb, yes, and not with anything else.
gershom:a7.1: Rather according to Rabbi Shimon: who did not speak of the Torah being particular at all; evidently he holds that one may also redeem it at its value.
gershom:a8.1: Rav Aḥa teaches it this way, “rather according to Rabbi Shimon.” Ravina found it difficult: how can he establish it according to Rabbi Shimon? We hold that [in a dispute of] Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon the halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.
gershom:a9.1: And moreover the tanna taught us an unattributed ruling in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: as we learned, “And a firstborn donkey is redeemed with a lamb, from sheep or from goats, etc.”: specifically with a lamb and not with anything else. And you say the halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, since you establish it according to Rabbi Shimon.
gershom:a10.1: Rather, even if you say Rabbi Yehuda: it is he who [holds] one redeems it at its value, for the redemption of a firstborn donkey should not be more stringent than the redemption of consecrated property; consecrated property is redeemed at its value with anything, and so too this. And when he says the Torah was particular about him with a lamb, this is what he holds: the Torah did not say “with a lamb” to be stringent with him, that is, with a lamb yes and with nothing else no; rather he may also redeem it with anything at its value. It said “with a lamb” only to be lenient with him: that if he wishes to redeem it with a lamb, even one worth only a danka, he may redeem it. In this the Torah was particular: that if he comes to redeem it for less than its value, he may redeem it only with a lamb.
gershom:a11.1: A dilemma was raised before them: is his redemption redeemed for the redeemer? That is, this one who redeemed it with a lamb, will the firstborn donkey be his?
gershom:a12.1: Or perhaps his redemption is redeemed for the owner: that is, the firstborn donkey is redeemed, but in any case the firstborn will be its owner’s and not the redeemer’s.
gershom:a13.1: Is it compared to consecrated property, and the Merciful One says, “And he will give the money and it will be assured to him”? That is, whoever redeems consecrated property, it is his; so too one who redeems a firstborn donkey, it is his.
gershom:a14.1: Or perhaps: even though benefit from it is forbidden like consecrated property, since its owner acquires this in-between amount, in that he can redeem a donkey worth a sela with a lamb worth a danka, it is not like consecrated property. For consecrated property is not redeemed for less than its value, while this in-between amount is the owner’s money; therefore all of it is the owner’s.
gershom:a15.1: And even though its owner has no right now to benefit from the donkey, [the thief] pays the double payment, as it is written: “for an ox, for a donkey, for a sheep, for a garment… he shall pay double” (Exodus 22:8).
gershom:a16.1: And why does he have no [right] now? Rabbi Shimon permits benefit from it before redemption!
gershom:a17.1: Rather, it is obviously Rabbi Yehuda. And if it enters your mind that it is compared to consecrated property, why does he pay the double payment to the owner? The Merciful One said: “And it be stolen from the man’s house… he shall pay double,” and not “stolen from the Temple”; and this firstborn donkey would be like consecrated property, so let him pay the principal and nothing more. Rather, since it teaches that he pays the double payment to the owner, conclude from it that it is the owner’s property, and its redemption is redeemed for the owner.
gershom:a18.1: You cannot say where it came into the possession of a priest: for example, where an Israelite gave this lamb to a priest as the redemption of a firstborn donkey, and the priest then sold it to an Israelite or gave it to him; in such a case it does not enter the pen, for we learned: “one that was purchased,” etc.
gershom:a19.1: Rather, an Israelite who had ten uncertain firstborn donkeys in his house, who designates ten lambs for them, brings them into the pen and tithes them, and they are his. And the same applies even if he had one or two uncertain firstborns and designated lambs for them to abrogate their uncertainty, and they are his: those lambs enter the pen with the other sheep to be tithed. And when he says “ten,” he tells us a novelty, that is, that they suffice for a tithe by themselves. He designates ten lambs for them, since they were originally an Israelite’s and now too came into an Israelite’s hand, and they are his, since they came to him by virtue of a priest.
gershom:a20.1: Smoothed untithed produce: made into a pile, whose processing for tithe is complete.
gershom:a21.1: He tithes them: because they were an Israelite’s, and now they are an Israelite’s. And they are his, since they came to him by virtue of a priest [the printed text reads “an Israelite,” corrected to “a priest”]. “They are his” means the money: he can sell the terumot to a priest and the tithes to a Levite, and the money will be his.
gershom:a22.1: And it was necessary to state both. For had he taught us the first one, [one would say] why he tithes them and they are his: because it stands separated. That is, since one redeems firstborn donkeys not with their own kind but with another kind, with lambs, these lambs that he designated for them are as if they were separated, as though his mother’s father, the priest, had separated them and they were his, and this Israelite inherited them from him; therefore they are his.
gershom:a23.1: But here: with smoothed untithed produce, since one must separate the tithe from the produce itself, say that gifts and tithes that were not separated are regarded as [not separated] while they were in the priest’s possession. Rather, say that now he must tithe them and give them to a priest. It teaches us: he tithes them and they are his.
gershom:a24.1: And had he taught us here, with untithed produce, [one would say] that he tithes them and they are his for this reason: because it is possible to tithe them from themselves, and it is as if they were separated from the moment they were smoothed, since once he smoothed it its tithes are at its side; and he inherited the untithed produce and the tithes from his mother’s father, the priest. Therefore he tithes, and they are his, for he can sell the tithes and the money is his. But there, with firstborn donkeys, since he must now bring a lamb from elsewhere and redeem each one, and cannot redeem them from themselves, we would not say that the lambs are as though separated and standing ever since they were the priest’s; rather, now he must separate them and give them to a priest. It teaches us that with lambs too we say “as if it stands separated”; therefore he separates them, tithes them, and they are his.
rashi:b1.1: And they are his: the teruma itself, and he sells it to priests.
rashi:b2.1: Your grain [degankha]: your smoothing [digunekha]. What you smooth is obligated in teruma, but not a gentile’s smoothing.
rashi:b3.1: That a Jew smoothed them from the gentile’s domain: the Jew was a sharecropper, and the land was the gentile’s.
rashi:b4.1: With regard to tithes: if they were tithed, we are not concerned that he exchanged them; or with regard to the Sabbatical Year, [we are not concerned] that he exchanged them for Sabbatical-Year produce, which would have to be removed [from the house] in the Sabbatical Year.
rashi:b5.1: As his produce: the gentile’s, for he certainly exchanged them, and he must separate tithe from them. This tanna holds that a gentile’s smoothing does not exempt, and it is a dispute in Menaḥot, in chapter Rabbi Yishmael (Menaḥot 66b).
rashi:b5.2: Demai: perhaps he exchanged them, perhaps he did not.
rashi:b6.1: To separate, everyone agrees: for even according to Rabbi Shimon, who says it is demai, out of the doubt one may not eat untithed produce, [for eating] which one is liable to death [at the hand of Heaven]; he must separate all of it, since it is like the demai of an am ha’aretz, from which one separates.
rashi:b6.2: And he needs to give them to a priest: below, the Gemara raises a difficulty from what we said above, “he tithes them and they are his.”
rashi:b6.3: Demai: and the burden of proof rests on the one who seeks to take from another, so the Israelite sells the teruma to a priest and the money is his. This demai is not like other demai, [from which] one gives the priest one part in a hundred [the teruma of the tithe]. There, there is a reason, as explained in Tractate Sota (48a): because an am ha’aretz thinks that it is the Levite whom the Merciful One commanded to give the teruma of the tithe, and not him. But here, the very uncertainty that exists with the teruma of the tithe exists with the great teruma as well.
rashi:b7.2: He tithes them and they are his: and we established it as a case where a Jew smoothed them in the gentile’s domain.
rashi:b8.1: With regard to great teruma: the first tanna and Rabbi Shimon disagree.
rashi:b8.2: With regard to teruma of the tithe: and they are his.
tosafot:b2.1: In brief: “Your grain,” says the Merciful One, and not the grain of a gentile. According to the one who expounds in Menaḥot, chapter Rabbi Yishmael (Menaḥot 67a), “your grain and not the grain of a gentile,” the question is well put: why does he tithe, if this grain grew and was smoothed in the gentile’s possession? Question: what is difficult here? Perhaps he holds like the one who says a gentile’s smoothing does not exempt, and “your grain” excludes smoothing by the Temple treasury. And if you say they disagree about a gentile’s smoothing only where the grain grew in a Jew’s possession, but where it grew in a gentile’s possession and the gentile smoothed it, it is exempt, still: perhaps it grew in a Jew’s possession. Answer: the Gemara understood that it speaks of grain grown in a gentile’s possession. But the discussion in Menaḥot (66b) proves they disagree even where it grew in a gentile’s possession; answer: the Gemara prefers to explain our case according to everyone. Further question: even if a gentile’s smoothing exempts, he should be obligated to tithe by rabbinic decree, on account of the wealthy [who would transfer their land to gentiles to evade tithes]. Answer: from “and they are his” the Gemara inferred that this view has no such decree, for then he would have to give it to a priest. This also answers the first question: “and they are his” shows he holds a gentile’s smoothing exempts, for otherwise let him give them to a priest. Remaining difficulty: let it say that even if it does not exempt, he need not give to a priest, since he says, “I come by virtue of a man with whom you cannot litigate”; and it is not reasonable that the one who holds the decree regarding the wealthy (who holds a gentile’s smoothing exempts) should obligate giving to a priest more than the one who holds it does not exempt. And what is implied shortly in our discussion, that he certainly must give to a priest (“with a gentile, it is like his produce,” implying that if he certainly exchanged them all agree he must give to a priest), is certainly according to the conclusion here: here, great teruma; there, teruma of the tithe. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b3.1: That a Jew smoothed them in the gentile’s possession: the Kuntres [Rashi] explained that the Jew was the gentile’s sharecropper. This is difficult for his explanation: if [he bought] the gentile’s share, that is smoothing by a gentile; if the Jew’s share, this is not buying untithed produce. It seems [better] to explain: a Jew smoothed them in the gentile’s possession after the Jew bought them. And this is what it means: one who buys untithed produce from a gentile, and it is now smoothed.
tosafot:b3.2: He tithes them, since there is no acquisition: this is puzzling. Even if there is acquisition, he is obligated to tithe them by rabbinic law, as is proven in HaKometz Rabba (Menaḥot 31a), in the discussion of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri about “go buy from a gentile and tithe for it.” And if you say [the Gemara] wants to find a Torah obligation, as a novelty, that even so he is obligated to tithe by Torah law: either way, a purchaser is exempt by Torah law, as is proven in chapter HaPo’alim (Bava Metzia 88b). However, according to Rabbeinu Tam’s explanation, that this applies only to one who buys after smoothing, but one who buys before smoothing and smooths it is obligated, it works out. Further, one can say: even if one who buys before smoothing is exempt by Torah law, there is still a novelty in that they are his although there is no acquisition; and there is no reason to exempt it on grounds of abrogation, since its prohibition is more severe, as is proven in HaKometz Rabba (Menaḥot 31a) from the question, “Let him tell him: go buy from a gentile,” and the answer that he holds there is no acquisition, so it would be [tithing] from the obligated for the exempt, even though [the obligation on] purchased produce is rabbinic.
tosafot:b4.1: They retain their presumptive status with regard to tithe and the Sabbatical Year: this implies that an ordinary am ha’aretz is suspected regarding the Sabbatical Year. So too in chapter Lulav HaGazul (Sukka 39a): one does not hand Sabbatical-Year money to an am ha’aretz; and in the first chapter of Ḥullin (6a): if he said, “Make it for me from yours,” he must be concerned about the leaven and the spices in it, on account of tithe and on account of the Sabbatical Year. But this is difficult from [the mishna]: the wife of a ḥaver may lend to the wife of an am ha’aretz, and a woman may lend to her friend who is suspected regarding the Sabbatical Year, which implies that ordinarily they are not suspected. I explained this in Ketubot (24a).
tosafot:b6.1: But if he certainly exchanged them, he must give them to a priest: even though we have heard that Rabbi Shimon holds a gentile’s smoothing exempts, he is nevertheless obligated on account of the decree regarding the wealthy, as I explained above.
tosafot:b9.1: In brief: Untithed produce that you buy from a gentile. This implies that a purchaser is obligated by Torah law, since a verse was needed to exempt him from teruma of the tithe. Rabbeinu Tam asked from chapter HaPo’alim (Bava Metzia 88b): “the produce of your seed,” and not a purchaser. He answered: one who buys before smoothing is obligated by Torah law. And the statement in chapter Rabbi Yishmael (Menaḥot 66b), that one may separate teruma from a gentile’s produce for a Samaritan’s and from anyone’s for anyone’s, [showing that] a gentile’s smoothing does not exempt, does not speak of one who buys from a gentile (for one who buys smoothed produce even from a Jew is exempt by Torah law), but of a gentile who separates from his own for a Jew’s, as we learned (Terumot 3:9): a gentile or a Samaritan who separated teruma, their teruma is teruma. And in chapter BeKhol Me’arvin (Eruvin 37b), on buying wine from Samaritans, “Torah law” may mean the teruma of grain, wine and oil. And even if every purchaser is exempt, our passage still works: it speaks of a gentile who tithed his produce and gave it to a Levite, and the Levite need not give teruma of the tithe to a priest; the tithe is a Torah obligation if there is no acquisition and a gentile’s smoothing does not exempt, and according to the one who says it exempts, he may have separated early, at the stage of ears. So the reason given above, “I come by virtue of a man with whom you cannot litigate,” holds: just as a Levite need not give teruma from a tithe that a gentile separates and gives him, so a Levite who buys untithed produce from a gentile and separates the tithe need not give its teruma of the tithe to a priest; otherwise, even though a purchaser is exempt by Torah law, he would have to give it by rabbinic law. Question: HaKometz Rabba (Menaḥot 31a) seems to support Rabbeinu Tam, since it calls such tithing “from the obligated for the exempt,” implying a Torah obligation. Answer: something mixed with a majority of non-sacred produce is called “obligated for exempt” even when the obligation is rabbinic, as the same passage says of buying from the market, calling it “from the obligated for the exempt” although demai is only rabbinic; whenever one side leans more toward obligation or exemption, it is called so. Further, that answer there (“he holds there is no acquisition”) applies only after smoothing. Question: after the Menaḥot passage, how does the Gemara know they disagree about whether a gentile’s smoothing exempts, rather than about whether a gentile has acquisition? Answer: then Rabbi Meir, who allows separating from anyone’s for anyone’s, would hold there is no acquisition, yet in Avoda Zara (21a) he holds there is acquisition, regarding not renting fields to gentiles lest they remove them from tithe; and the Jerusalem Talmud, which does frame it as a dispute about acquisition, does not explain the Avoda Zara mishna as being about abrogating tithe. One can also infer from Rabbi Yehuda, who allows separating from anyone’s for anyone’s (Menaḥot 66b) and holds there is acquisition in chapter HaMekabel (Bava Metzia 101a), according to Rabbeinu Tam’s explanation of one who leases his ancestral field from a gentile; and the Avoda Zara case can be explained as a different kind of abrogation. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b1.1: Rather, that a Jew smoothed them from the gentile’s domain: for example, the gentile gave the Jew his field to work for a share of the crop, and the Jew smoothed them. And “the one who purchases” that it says means that the Jew acquires them from him through the labor of his work. And they are his, in that he can sell them and take the money.
gershom:b2.1: For he says to the priest: “I come, etc.”
gershom:b3.1: In their presumptive status for tithes and for the Sabbatical Year: that is, if one [the printed text reads “a priest”] deposited his tithed produce, there is no concern that [the depositary] exchanged them and returns untithed produce to him; rather he returns the very ones that were deposited with him. And likewise for the Sabbatical Year: if he deposited with him produce of the sixth year and he returns it in the Sabbatical Year, there is no concern that he exchanged it and returns Sabbatical-Year produce, which may not be traded and must be removed once it has ceased [from the field] for the wild animals. Rather, he returns the very ones that were deposited with him, for he would not want to cause him to stumble.
gershom:b4.1: With a gentile: but if he deposited them with a gentile, when he returns them they are like his produce. They have the law of the gentile’s produce, for we say he certainly exchanged them and returned others; and their law is like produce that a Jew smoothed from the gentile’s domain, from which he must separate great teruma and give it to a priest, while the rest, the first tithe and the teruma of the tithe, he tithes and they are his.
gershom:b5.1: Rabbi Shimon says: they have the status of demai, since perhaps he exchanged them and perhaps he did not. Therefore he tithes them and they are his, for he does not give even the great teruma to a priest but sells it. And as for separating the great teruma, all agree that he must separate it; when they disagree is about giving it to a priest, with regard to great teruma alone. The first tanna holds, etc. And Rabbi Shimon holds that it is uncertain whether he exchanged them or not; therefore he separates the great teruma, and they are his, and he sells it to a priest.
gershom:b6.1: And he stated this teaching: of Rabbi Elazar.
gershom:b7.1: Perhaps it is not difficult. What Abaye inferred, that if he certainly exchanged them all agree he must give them to a priest, is here, with great teruma; that is, it speaks of great teruma alone. And what Shmuel bar Natan said, “he tithes them and they are his,” speaks of teruma of the tithe and not of great teruma. Abaye said to Rav Dimi: It is surely as you answer me, “perhaps here, great teruma, and there, teruma of the tithe”: for when he certainly exchanged them, all agree that great teruma must be given to a priest; and as for one who buys untithed produce from a gentile, where it says “he tithes them and they are his,” it speaks of teruma of the tithe, which he is exempt from giving to a priest [for nothing; the printed text has an unclear word here], as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi expounds this verse: untithed produce that you buy from an Israelite, etc.
gershom:b8.1: And if it dies: the lamb that he separated for a firstborn donkey, before it came into the priest’s possession, the priest may benefit from it, for from the moment he separated it, it stands in the priest’s possession.
